package.title: Tirzepatide and Alcohol: Can It Cause Low Blood Sugar? #shorts
package.description:
The tirzepatide label says taking it with insulin or a sulfonylurea may raise low blood sugar risk. The NHS says drinking a lot, especially without eating, can cause lows with diabetes medicines.
Signs: shakiness, sweating, dizziness, a fast heartbeat. Passing out, a seizure, or not responding normally? Call your local emergency number right away.
We can't name a safe amount of alcohol. Don't change your medicines on your own.
Sources: Zepbound Prescribing Information, Eli Lilly (revised 8/2026) https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf | Zepbound Medication Guide, Eli Lilly (revised 28 Aug 2026) https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-us-mg.pdf | NHS, Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia), reviewed 03 Aug 2023 https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/low-blood-sugar-hypoglycaemia/
#Tirzepatide #GLP1 #Hypoglycemia
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate, safe and inside the tight length arm. I counted 119 spoken words by hand, matching the note (s1 12, s2 14, s3 16, s4 9, s5 15, s6 30, s7 23), and the first sentence is 9 words.

**Claims checked:**
- **Label (s2):** The Zepbound label says using it with insulin or an insulin secretagogue such as a sulfonylurea may raise the risk of low blood sugar (sections 5.7 and 7.1). The script's "may raise low sugar risk" matches.
- **NHS on alcohol (s3):** The NHS page says lows can happen in people with diabetes who "drink a lot of alcohol, particularly without eating". It also says low blood sugar "usually affects people with diabetes who take insulin or some other diabetes medicines". s3 keeps that scope.
- **Symptom list (s4):** Sweating, shaking, dizziness and palpitations all appear on the NHS page. "Fast heartbeat" is also standard Medication Guide wording.
- **Emergency line (s5):** The NHS says to call 999 if someone has very low blood sugar and isn't responding normally, and notes when they've been drinking alcohol. s5 has no source tag, uses "your local emergency number" so it works in all four markets, and keeps "right away".
- **Safety and closing lines (s6, s7):** They're in the right order with no "safe amount", and the Exp F line and closing line are both there.

**One minor fix:** the s2 fact card says "heavy drinking can add to it". That suggests an added effect with tirzepatide, which no source states.

**Notes on sources:**
- Both Lilly PDFs load (about 989 KB and 197 KB), but their text couldn't be extracted. I confirmed the label wording from the FDA label search results instead.
- The NHS page still shows "last reviewed 03 Aug 2023", with its review due 03 Aug 2026. That's the live date, so it's listed correctly, but it's overdue.
- I couldn't find "seizure" in the NHS text I pulled. It's reasonable general safety advice and isn't tagged to a source, so I'm not flagging it.

There's nothing about dosing, nothing telling people to change medicines, and the hook pays off by about 6 seconds.

issues.claim: NHS: heavy drinking can add to it.
issues.problem: "Add to it" suggests alcohol stacks with tirzepatide's own low-sugar risk. The NHS page says drinking a lot, especially without eating, can cause lows in people with diabetes. It says nothing about tirzepatide. That makes the card a little stronger than the narration and the source, which fails the muted-viewer test.
issues.fix: Replace the fact text with: "Label: low blood sugar risk is higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea. NHS: a lot of alcohol, especially without food, can cause lows with diabetes medicines."

issues.claim: Myth: drinking on tirzepatide can't drop blood sugar. Sometimes it can.
issues.problem: The opening card doesn't say who this applies to. A muted viewer could read it as saying that drinking on tirzepatide lowers blood sugar for everyone, which neither source shows. The narration narrows it to insulin and sulfonylureas within about 6 s, so this is minor, but the title and the card could carry the scope sooner.
issues.fix: Optional: change the s1 on-screen text to "Myth: drinking on tirzepatide can't drop blood sugar. With some diabetes medicines, it can." and leave the narration as it is.
